LYNCHEDINDAYLIGHT
An Ohio Negro Who Murdered an Octogenarian Banker.
THE RETRIBUTION VERY SWIFT.
Less Than Four Hours After the Murder the Black Man Was Swinging on the Tree.
Cincinnati, Aug. 21.—At New Richmond, Ohio, twenty-five miles up the Ohio river from Cincinnati, at 4 o'clock this afternoon a mob took Noah Anderson, colored, from the jail and hanged him for the murder of Franklin Friedman, nearly 80 years old and president of the First National bank of that place. Mr. Friedman was among the wealthiest men in Clearmont county. He owned a number of farms, and lived at Clearmontville, about two miles from New Richmond. He was driving to New Richmond shortly after noon today, when he stopped at one of his houses. Hitching his horse at the door, he went into an adjoining field, where he was suddenly attacked by Anderson, a muscular negro, who had no weapon but his hands. With these he quickly bore the aged banker to the earth, and then, clutching his throat with the power of a madman, he literally choked his helpless victim to death.

When Friedman was dead Anderson fled. He was soon captured, however, and taken to jail. A mob gathered and Anderson was hanged to a tree.

CINCINNATI, August 21.—At New Richmond, Ohio, twenty-five miles up the Ohio river from Cincinnati, at 4 o'clock this afternoon, a mob took Noah Anderson, colored, from the jail and hanged him for the murder to-day of Franklin Friedman, nearly eighty years old, and President of the First National Bank of that place.

Mr. Friedman was among the wealthiest men in Clermont county. He owns a number of farms at Clermontville, about two miles from New Richmond. He was driving into New Richmond shortly after noon to-day, when he stopped at one of the houses. Hitching his horse at the door yard, he went into an adjoining field, where he was suddenly attacked by Noah Anderson, a muscular negro, who had no weapon but his hands. With these he quickly bore the aged banker to the earth, and then clutching his throat with the power of a demon, he literally choked his helpless victim to death.

It was not long until Anderson was captured and taken to the New Richmond jail, where a great crowd quickly gathered. Anderson made no attempt to conceal his crime. He gloatingly told all the details and said he had given the old man what he deserved. It is said that Anderson was not right in his mind and that one of his hallucinations was that Briedman had deprived him of a large sum of money. The truth is the two men had no dealings together, as Anderson came to New Richmond on a shanty boat only a few months ago and claimed to be a paper hanger.

The crowd became greatly excited. As the negro's confession became known, cries of "lynch him," "hang the coward," arose. A rope was brought, and the end seemed near. Prominent citizens addressed the mob, counseling moderation.

Anderson was in his cell on his knees crying for mercy. The marshal when a momentary lull came, attempted to take Anderson to a more secure jail, at Batavia, the county seat. No sooner did the man appear outside the jail than the freuzied mob rushed at the marshal and seizing the prisoner, bore him quickly to the nearest tree and in a brief time he was dead.

There was no masking, no attempt at concealment. Every person present had engaged in the mob and knew all the others. It was simply an act of frenzy under most aggravating circumstances.
noah-anderson-new-richmond-1895-08-21.A4: THERE is some justification for the lynching in the South of the brutal but sane negro who outrages a white girl, but why a crazy negro should be lynched in Ohio for killing an old white man, is what only the large republican majority in that State can tell.

THE MOB LAY IN WAIT. A Negro Murderer Taken from County Officials and Lynched.
NEW RICHMOND, Ky., Aug. 21.—Franklin Fridman, aged 80, the wealthiest man in Claremont county and President of the First National Bank of New Richmond, was murdered yesterday afternoon by a negro, Noah Anderson. Mr. Fridman lived at Claremontville, and was on his way to New Richmond in his buggy when Anderson sprang out from a place of concealment on the roadside. He seized Mr. Fridman by the throat and choked him to death. The murderer fled, but was soon captured and locked in the New Richmond jail.

Immediately after being put in jail early this morning shouts of "Hang him!" aroused the community. By 3 o'clock the mob had quieted down, and the Marshal tried to take the prisoner to the county jail at Batavia. The mob lay in wait, wrested the negro from the officers, dragged him a square away, and hanged him to a tree.
noah-anderson-new-richmond-1895-08-21.A18: The negro lynched in Claremont county richly deserved death, but he deserved it at the hands of the law, not at the hands of a mob. If he had been tried he would certainly have been convicted and hanged, so that there was no excuse in the uncertainty of justice. The men who did the lynching took no trouble to disguise themselves. If the authorities want them they will be found easily, but probably no jury could be found to convict them, for public sentiment is with them. This is unfortunate for Claremont county.
noah-anderson-new-richmond-1895-08-21.A23: Oh! ho! Ohio white men took a negro murderer from jail Tuesday last and lynched him. By all means they should have kept the peaee and dignity of the state so politicans and papers there might keep up their tirade of abuse against the south for such "outrages."
noah-anderson-new-richmond-1895-08-21.A24:
HE WAS FROM KANSAS.
The Negro Lynched at New Richmond was Citizen of Newton.
Noah Anderson the negro lynched at New Richmond, Ohio, a few days ago lived at Newton for a number of years and was subject to fits of insanity. He entertained an idea that someone had dispossessed him of a large sum of money and it is supposed that he believed Friedman was the man who did so. Anderson was a paper hanger by trade. That he was suffering from a return of the disease of insanity there is no doubt. He was adjudged insane by Probate Judge N. C. Groom at Newton in November, 1892, and was taken to the state insane asylum December 1, 1892, but remained less than a year, escaping from the institution at Osawatomie November 8, 1893. He was discharged from the asylum May 10, 1894, but the record says: "Discharge not in his right mind." He visited Newton just after his discharge and was there for several weeks. He left for the east last summer and had not been heard of until the news of the murder and lynching was received.

STRANGLED BY AN OHIO; MOB. Negro Murderer Dragged to His Death Through New Richmond's Streets.
Cincinnati, O., Aug. 21.—The third lynching in the history of Ohio took place this afternoon at New Richmond, twenty miles up the Ohio river from Cincinnati. Noah Anderson, a negro, was taken from the marshal and mayor by a mob and strangled to death. At 12:30 o'clock Anderson murdered Franklin Friedman, and three and a half hours later he was dangling from a tree a half a square from the village jail.

The murder occurred while Friedman was on his way home from New Richmond. He stopped to look at some land adjoining a lot where the murderer lived. Anderson, who had frequently threatened to kill any one who came near his house, came out and ordered the old man away. The latter replied that he was on his own property and would not leave until he got ready. Anderson rushed upon him bore him to the ground and choked him until life was gone.

A neighbor gave the alarm and the police authorities went to Anderson's house. It is just on the outskirts of New Richmond. They found him, apparently unconcerned. He was taken to the New Richmond jail, a small, frail affair, and locked up. Half a hundred men followed, and soon the mob feeling developed from the discussion of the terrible crime. The jail was surrounded by several hundred people, who shouted, "Hang him! Lynch the coward!" Anderson divined the purpose of the mob, and his murderous heart failed him, and he raved in his cell and pleaded for mercy. Shortly after Anderson's arrest he confessed to Marshal Henderson, of New Richmond, that he committed the murder, and gave as his reason that Friedman was the cause of his losing over $200,000,000. He said that Friedman scratched around and resisted while he strangled him, but it did no good.

STRANGLED IN THE DUST.

About 4 o'clock the crowd that surrounded the jail were almost furious, and the marshal who attempted to enter the jail, was kept back by the mob. Finally he was allowed to enter the jail in company with Mayor Dawson. They brought Anderson forth to take him to the county jail at Batavia, but no sooner had they reached the sidewalk than a man threw a rope around Anderson's neck, at the same time crying, "This is no bluff; we must have him." Strong arms immediately grasped the rope, and in an instant Anderson was pulled forward and fell on his face in the dusty street. The mob then began to run north on Washington street, with the murderer trailing in the dust. At the corner of Washington and Western avenues the mob stopped and threw the rope across the limb of a large poplar tree. The crowd evidently weakened at the last moment, but one man, who appeared to be the leader, cried out, "You're a nice lot of nervy fellows," and with this he jerked the body upward and tied the end of the rope to the trunk of the tree. The negro was evidently dead when he was strung up, as he showed no signs of life, having been no doubt strangled to death in the dust.

Friedman was one of the wealthiest men of Clermont county, and leaves an estate valued at $250,000. He was born at Stolhaven, near Strazburg, Germany, in 1816, and came to the United States in 1833, locating in Cincinnati, where he was engaged as a boiler maker for some years. In 1840 he removed to Clermontville, Clermont county, O. where he has since been engaged in mercantile, manufacturing and banks.

Train Robbers' Desperate Attempt to Blow Open a Safe.

Omaha, Neb., Aug. 21.—The east bound Union Pacific flyer, due in Omaha at 10:25 this morning, was held up by train robbers in a cut between Brady's island and Gothenburg about 1 o'clock this morning and the Pacific express robbed of about $130, found in the small way station safe. The robbers flagged the train, and when it stopped boarded the engine. They then climbed on the small end of the car as the train was leaving Brady Island.

When the train reached the switch at the east end of the station the robbers clambered up on the tank and engine and covered Engineer Austin and Fireman Duke with their guns, and ordered them to run the train ahead until commanded to stop. They compelled the engineer and fireman to uncouple the express and baggage car from the train and to run them ahead. They compelled the engineera and fireman to pound on the doors of the car and tell the baggageman and expressman to open it. One bandit entered the car with dynamite, while the other one visible guarded the engineer and fireman. A third is supposed to have been outside watching the train it still being coupled to the express car and train men coming out to see the cause of the stop.

While this scene was being enacted, robber No. 2 was guarding the engineer and fireman on the outside with revolvers and a Winchester. Robber No. 1 asked the fireman to hand him the dynamite, which was on the tender, which he did. The dynamite was placed in position on the big safe, a fuse attached and a quantity of waste packed around it. The match was then applied. The expressman was ordered out of the car, and the robbers and three train men walked a short distance away and all laid down on the ground.

At this time the engineer asked he robbers to allow him to turn off the injector so as to prevent his engine from blowing up. The fireman was allowed to go forward to the engine and instead of turning off the injector, the fireman cut the steam and air pipes and bell cords, detaching the engine from the train and turned on full steam and started for Gothenburg for assistance. The explosion followed almost upon the departure of the engine. The robber who entered the car appeared, and discovering the engine gone, said that the business was a failure all around and called to his companions to fellow him. The three men then escaped in the darkness, and mounting horses they rode away.

After the explosion the train crew entered the baggage car, and with considerable effort put out the fire which was kindled by the explosion. Seven trunks and contents were demolished by the explosion. The big fire and burglar proof safe was not seriously damaged. The top was slightly disfigured. The fire proof packing was disarranged and a hole about six inches in depth was made in it where the dynamite was placed, reaching to the steel cover. One of the steel bands which holds the safe in position, about an inch in thickness and a foot in length, was rent in two and hurled a distance of ten feet, penetrating a trunk. The Pacific Express packages of freight were undisturbed at the front end of the car. The total damage to the car and contents will not exceed $1,000.

Lynching in Ohio
Daniel A. Long, pro
Lynching in Ohio
Rev. Daniel A. Long, president of Antioch College, took the train here this morning, says the Greensboro Record of Monday, in response to startling intelligence just received. Miss Grace Friedland, an assistant professor in Antioch College, had been conveyed by her father, an old and wealthy farmer, to visit a neighbor; the old gentleman was returning home unattended, and at a certain point on the way he was assaulted by a colored man and choked to death. The colored man was promptly arrested and jailed at New Richmond, the county seat of Claremont county. A mob was collected quickly and in defiance of every remonstrance the murderer was taken out and hanged to the limb of a sycamore tree. This is the second lynching of colored men near New Richmond within the past two years.

We know it is a difficult task, but try to be good, honest and happy.

SATURDAY, AUGUST 31, 1895.

"What constitutes race leadership, anyhow?" asks the New York Age. Brains.

Our sympathies are with the taxpayers of Wichita who must put up for the prohibition crusade being carried on there.

We would suggest that Ed Hackley be put on the next Colorado state ticket as a representative of the colored people.

For fear that our people will run short on names when speaking of the colored man, we suggest that blackamoor be brought into use.

The State University opens next month. Our young ladies and gentlemen should avail themselves of the many advantages offered, and enter.

Some people think that to rise they must undermine others. No man can rise to permanent success in this life over the dead bodies of others.

The Prohibitionists of other cities will have all they can do if they regulate their drug-store joints. We don't need any missionaries over here.

The Woman's Era for this month is a John W. Jacks issue. In all seriousness, who is Jacks? A detective should be employed and sent to Missouri to find out.

The little fellow who masquerades as editor of the Courant would starve in 30 days should the proprietors of that paper turn him out upon the world. No other paper would have him and he could not earn a living.

The people of the East will realize some of these days that there is a South and a West to this country and that those sections propose to be heard. Bimetallism suits the South and West, and bimetallism it must be in '96.

THE HERALD has received the proceedings of the sixth annual meeting of the Northeastern District Missionary Baptist association, the convention of which took place in Atchison in July of this year. The proceedings are nicely arranged in book form.

THE HERALD favors sound money that has a gold and silver basis. The ratio existing between the two metals should be sufficient to maintain the parity of each. Then all debts in the United States, including government bonds, should be paid in either gold or silver.

Twelve colored men lynched a colored man at Springfield, Ky., this week; four men were strung up in Yreka, Cal., this week; a Negro had his life taken by a mob in Ohio last week, and so on. Still some fool named M. D. Conway says lynchings in the United States have ceased.

The colored exhibit of the Atlanta Exposition promises to be the grandest thing in the history of the colored people since the war and it will reflect credit on its managers, their assistants and the colored people of the world. The Southern Negro has the right idea of progress.

The writer of today, who tries to engender race antipathy, who endeavors to make the white race hate the colored, or vice versa, is an enemy to mankind. Every effort should be made to create a friendly feeling, a common cause, and to show by practical works the brotherhood of man.

The colored people of Colorado are moving along the right line; they are organizing and calling meetings to secure lands and water rights. Every colored man in the state should take an interest in this move. The hope and future success of the colored people in this country are on the farm.

City life is too rich for the blood of our people. It is sapping the very life-blood from us and is producing a nomadic class of laborers. We must leave the city and go to the farm. When we become an intelligent, progressive, farming element, we will be respected; and owning land will have an influence which will be a power in every community.

Some prohibition crank came over here, went away and reported that there were but 1,900 Christians as church members in this city. We like to respect ministers, but this one certainly lied. There are about 1,500 colored Christians and 4,000 white Christians, making a total of 5,500 in a population of 22,000, or one-fourth of the city's population belong to church.

The Prohibitionists do everything possible to induce the Republicans to inaugurate a prohibition war, then when election time comes they put a ticket in the field and do everything they can to defeat the Republicans. In addition to this they do not give the Republicans credit for anything they do. There is not a Prohibitionist in the state that gives Governor Morrill any credit for his attempts to enforce the prohibitory law.

Even if Ohio does have a lynching now and then, the colored people of that state are very progressive. Cleveland can boast of a colored state Senator and two colored men in the state Legislature, and she also has colored street car conductors, motormen and colored women milliners in the millinery departments of stores run by white people. "But with all of this individual advancement and progressiveness," says a writer in the Cleveland Gazette, "the colored people of Cleveland are sadly lacking and behind the colored people of the South, so far as race organizations are concerned, for business enterprises."

The bond syndicate cannot keep the Gold Reserve up to its proper place as long as imports are paid for in gold. The value of imports so far exceeds that of exports that the balance of trade with Europe is against us, thus producing a constant drainage of gold from the United States' treasury. The only remedy to maintain a Gold Reserve, or any other kind of a financial reserve, is for the United States to pay for all imports in either gold or silver, at the option of the United States. Let foreign nations that do not wish to take either gold or silver keep out of our markets. The right kind of bimetallism will solve the question.

One by one the old philanthropists are passing beyond the river into the Great Unknown. It is always painful for us to chronicle the death of the very humblest, and especially is it very sad to us to mention the death of humanitarians—those who can see in nature the "Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of Man." A few weeks ago Judge S. O. Thacher of Lawrence passed from time into eternity. He was a man in every sense of the word—broad, liberal, sympathetic and very philanthropic. His sympathies were always with those who were contending against the odds in life. We often think that such as he are spared, being allotted a long life to accomplish certain purposes in the world. Judge Thacher was true to all the higher motives that govern the actions of men. In his death the state loses one of its best citizens.
